engine: markdown
title: "Pipelines"
---

```{term}
#| include: false
rush run -o mtcars.csv 'mtcars'
```

The real power of `rush` is combining commands in Unix pipelines. Because `rush`
reads from stdin and writes to stdout by default, it composes naturally with
other command-line tools, including other `rush` invocations.

## Chaining rush commands

Filter with `rush run`, then query with SQL:

```{term}
rush run 'dplyr::filter(df, cyl == 8)' mtcars.csv | \
  rush sql "SELECT COUNT(*) AS n, ROUND(AVG(mpg), 1) AS avg_mpg FROM stdin" -
```

Query with SQL, then filter further with `rush run`:

```{term}
rush sql "SELECT mpg, hp, wt FROM mtcars WHERE hp > 200" mtcars.csv | \
  rush run 'head(df, 5)' -
```

## JSON in pipelines

Produce JSON, process it, and convert back to CSV:

```{term}
rush run -O json 'head(df, 3)' mtcars.csv | rush run -F json 'dplyr::select(df, mpg, hp, wt)' -
```

## Format conversion in pipelines

Read CSV, filter with SQL, output as JSON:

```{term}
rush sql -O json "SELECT cyl, hp, mpg FROM mtcars WHERE hp > 150 LIMIT 5" mtcars.csv
```

## Multiple rush commands

Chain `rush run` to progressively transform data:

```{term}
rush run 'dplyr::select(df, mpg, cyl, hp, wt)' mtcars.csv | \
  rush run 'dplyr::filter(df, hp > 200)' -
```

## With other tools

`rush` plays well with standard Unix tools:

```{term}
rush run 'df' mtcars.csv | wc -l
```

```{term}
rush run 'df' mtcars.csv | cut -d, -f2 | sort | uniq -c
```

Feed external data into rush:

```bash
curl -s https://api.example.com/data.json | rush run -F json 'head(df)'
```

```{term}
#| include: false
rm -f mtcars.csv
```
